Aggregation: Chapter one. Aggregation: when one household is exact.

Start with three households, Ada, Ben and Cleo, with incomes of twenty, sixty and a hundred and twenty. Suppose each spends a fixed amount plus half of every extra dollar: straight Engel curves with the same slope. Their total spending is 136. Now Cleo gives Ada twenty. Cleo spends ten less, Ada ten more, and the total does not move. Whatever the distribution of income, total spending depends only on total income. In this economy one household could stand for all three.

Now give them different slopes, as real households have. Ada, with little, spends nine tenths of an extra dollar; Ben, six tenths; Cleo, three tenths. Total spending starts at 126. The same transfer: Cleo spends six less, Ada eighteen more, and total spending rises by twelve. Same total income, different total spending. Now the distribution matters, and no single household can stand for the three.

William Gorman stated the condition in 1953. If every household's spending is a straight line in its income, and the lines have the same slope, the same marginal propensity to spend, then total spending depends only on total income, and a single representative household reproduces the aggregate exactly. It is a knife-edge. It fails as soon as the poor spend a larger share of an extra dollar than the rich, and they do.

Here is that fact inside the economy this part will build, in which households face income risk they cannot insure. The curves show how much of a small windfall a household spends within the year, against its wealth. A household with nothing saved and the lowest wage spends about 76 percent of it, and the share falls steeply as savings build up. A household with the highest wage spends little even with nothing saved: it is busy building a buffer while times are good. Averaged over the population it is 7 percent, against about 4 percent for a representative household, who spends only the interest on a windfall. The slopes differ, so Gorman's condition fails, and the distribution of wealth becomes part of the state of the economy.
Incomplete: The models of this part start from one change to the textbook. Each household's income jumps between bad years and good ones, and there is no insurance to buy against it: no contract pays out when your own income falls. The only way to smooth is to save in a single asset, a bond, and there is a limit on how much can be borrowed. With complete insurance, consumption would be flat and one household would stand for all. Without it, each household self-insures by saving, and its own history of luck decides how much it holds. Truman Bewley studied such households in the late 1970s; Mark Huggett put them into a market in 1993.

Why does this matter for interest rates? Start from the household's Euler equation. Today's marginal utility is at least the discounted, interest-weighted marginal utility expected tomorrow, with equality unless the household is pinned at its borrowing limit. Give it the interest rate a representative household would face, where patience exactly offsets interest. Then expected marginal utility can only fall over time. But income risk keeps knocking consumption around, so marginal utility can only stop falling once the household is so rich that the risk no longer matters. Wealth drifts up without bound: at that interest rate, everyone wants to save, and nobody wants to borrow. So the market can only clear at a lower rate. Uninsurable risk pushes the interest rate below the rate of time preference.

Huggett's economy makes this concrete. Households lend to and borrow from one another, so their bond holdings must add up to zero. The curve shows the total they want to hold at each interest rate. At low rates, borrowers outweigh savers. As the rate rises toward the rate of time preference, five percent, the precautionary demand for bonds explodes, exactly as the Euler equation said. The market clears where the curve crosses zero, at 3.19 percent. Huggett used this to ask whether uninsured risk could explain why safe interest rates are so low; with a tight enough limit on borrowing, it pushes them a long way down.

In equilibrium, the households spread out. Those with low incomes run down their bonds and borrow; those with high incomes build them up. And a crowd of low-income households sits exactly at the borrowing limit, with nothing left to borrow: they would spend any extra dollar. The interest rate, the amount saved, and the response to any shock all depend on this whole picture, not on an average household.
Aiyagari: In 1994 Rao Aiyagari put such households into the growth model. Households maximize expected lifetime utility. Each year they earn a wage times a personal draw that is persistent and cannot be insured, earn interest on their savings, and cannot borrow. Firms rent capital and labour and pay each its marginal product, as in Part twenty. And the market for capital clears when the savings of all households, added up over their stationary distribution, equal the capital firms use. The numbers here: a discount factor of 0.96 a year, risk aversion of three, wage draws with persistence 0.9, capital's share 0.36, depreciation eight percent.

The household's rules, found by the endogenous grid method of Part fifty-one. On the left, consumption against wealth for the lowest, middle and highest wage. At the bottom, the low-wage household spends everything it has: the borrowing limit binds. The curves are steep there and flatten as wealth grows: the more you have, the less a dollar more changes what you spend. On the right, next year's wealth against this year's. Above the dashed diagonal the household saves; below it, it runs its savings down. A good year pushes it up, a bad year pulls it down: wealth is a buffer, filled in good years and drained in bad ones.

Now the market for capital. Firms want more capital the cheaper it is: the pink curve. Households, computed at each interest rate, supply the green curve. It rises slowly at first, then shoots up as the rate approaches the rate of time preference, for the reason of the last chapter. A representative household would supply any amount at exactly 4.17 percent, the dashed line, and the economy would settle at capital of 5.45. With many households the curves cross at 2.12 percent, with capital of 7.26. That is 33 percent more capital, built by households saving against risks they cannot insure, and a saving rate of 28 percent. Aiyagari's question was how much of a nation's saving is precautionary; in this economy, a good deal.
Island: Chapter four. The Island's hundred thousand households.

The rules are now known, so the Island can be populated. Give a hundred thousand households the equilibrium rules, draw each one's luck, and let them live. Here are five of them, followed for two centuries. A run of good years carries one up; a run of bad years drains its buffer to zero. The dashed line is the economy's capital per household. No household stays rich or poor for ever. The distribution settles down; the people inside it keep moving.

After four hundred years of simulated time, here is the whole crowd: wealth across all hundred thousand households. A wealth Gini of 0.48, the top one percent holding 4.7 percent, and 1.6 percent of households at the borrowing limit. The same numbers come from a different calculation with no random draws at all: Young's method from Part fifty-one, which moves the whole histogram forward at once, splitting each household's savings between the two nearest grid points. The two agree to the second or third digit. The simulation is what the economy looks like; the histogram is how it is computed.

Aiyagari's own table varied three things: how widely wages are spread, how persistent they are, and how much households dislike risk. Here it is, recomputed with the methods of Part fifty-one. With a small spread and no persistence, the rate is barely below the rate of time preference: a bad year is soon over, and a little saving covers it. Raise the spread, the persistence and the risk aversion, and the rate falls, as households pile up buffers: down to 0.72 percent with persistence 0.9 and risk aversion 5. Every cell is below the rate of time preference. Uninsured risk lowers interest rates, and the more persistent the risk, the more it lowers them.
PlayIt: Chapter five. Play it: rates fall.

Your turn. The central bank cuts the real interest rate by a quarter of a point, starting next quarter, and lets the cut fade over about a year. The economy is the Island's: households hold about 4 quarters of income in savings they can use, they spend on average 22 percent of a windfall within the quarter, and output is whatever they buy. Line the households up by wealth and cut them into fifths. Which fifth raises its spending the most in the first quarter, as a share of what it spent before? The poorest, the second fifth, the middle, or the richest? Pause, and choose.

Here is the first quarter. Every fifth spends more, but not equally. The largest rise is in the second fifth: 1.18 percent. The richest fifth raise their spending least, by 0.76 percent, and the poorest by 0.95. Across everyone, spending rises 0.91 percent. If you chose the poorest, you were close, and for an interesting reason: their rise comes almost entirely from somewhere other than the interest rate.

Split each bar in two. The blue part is the direct effect: how each fifth would respond to the lower rate if its income did not change. The gold part is the indirect effect: other households spend more, firms produce more, and incomes rise. For the poorest fifth, the direct effect is almost nothing, 0.04 percent. They are at or near their borrowing limit: a cheaper loan they cannot take means little to them, but a fatter paycheque is spent at once. The richest fifth respond mostly to the rate itself, and their pay is a small part of their resources. And the two groups who matter most for spending own almost none of the wealth: the poorest two fifths hold 1 percent of it. A representative household, who owns the average wealth, cannot see any of this.
Wealth: How well does this economy match the distribution of wealth in the data? In the Federal Reserve's distributional accounts for the United States, the richest one percent of households hold 32.5 percent of all wealth, and the richest tenth 69 percent. In Aiyagari's economy, the top one percent hold 4.7 percent. The model gets a spread of wealth, but not the very rich. Saving against bad luck builds a buffer of a few years' income, and then stops: once the buffer is full, there is no reason to keep accumulating. The rich in the data are not buffer-stock savers.

Here is why. The curves show how much each household adds to its wealth in a year, as a share of what it has. A poor household with a low wage runs its wealth down; one with a high wage builds it up quickly. But above some level, every curve falls below zero: even the luckiest household runs its wealth down. The interest rate is below the rate of time preference, so wealth for its own sake is not worth keeping. Nothing in the model lets fortunes grow without limit, and so nothing produces the long upper tail of the data.

Three fixes have been tried. The first gives households different patience: Krusell and Smith let the discount factor itself drift between values. With three permanent types here, the top one percent hold 6.9 percent: better, but nowhere near. The second, after Jess Benhabib, Alberto Bisin and Shenghao Zhu, gives some households, at some times, a higher return on their wealth: think of an owner whose business takes off. If 9 percent of households at a time earn six points more, the top one percent hold 7.5 percent; if they earn eight points more, 23.4 percent. Returns that compound for the lucky few make fortunes that grow until the luck ends, and that is what the data's upper tail looks like. The third fix, not shown, gives the best-paid a small chance of extraordinary earnings.

On a log-log plot of how many households are richer than each level of wealth, a Pareto tail is a straight line, and the flatter the line, the fatter the tail. Aiyagari's economy has a steep, thin tail: an exponent of about 5. With returns six points higher for the lucky, about 2.9; with eight points, about 1.5. The data's top shares imply 1.5. Notice how sensitive the tail is: two points of extra return move the top one percent's share from 8 to 23 percent. A model can match the top this way, but only by choosing returns that must then be measured, and measuring returns to private wealth is hard.
KrusellSmith: Chapter seven. Aggregate shocks: Krusell and Smith.

So far the economy has been in a steady state. Now let it have booms and recessions: aggregate productivity switches between good and bad times, and unemployment rises in the bad ones. To decide how much to save, a household must forecast next year's wages and interest rates. Those depend on next year's capital, which depends on how much every household saves, which depends on the whole distribution of wealth today, and on how that distribution will move. The state of the economy includes a distribution: in principle, infinitely many numbers. Krusell and Smith made a bet: let households forecast using only the average, and then check whether anything better was available.

The algorithm is a loop. Guess a rule that forecasts next quarter's capital from this quarter's, one for good times and one for bad. Solve every household's problem as if the rule were true, by the endogenous grid method. Simulate the economy for a thousand quarters, moving the whole distribution forward. Regress the simulated capital on its own past to get a new rule, and go round again until the rule stops changing. Here it took 30 rounds and 34 seconds, in the calibration that a comparison of methods made standard in 2010.

How good is a forecast that uses only the mean? The white line is capital in the simulated economy, with every household's choices in it; the grey bands are bad times. The usual measure of fit is the regression's R-squared, and it is 0.999980 in good times and 0.999977 in bad: almost perfect. Wouter den Haan pointed out that R-squared flatters a rule that is only ever asked one quarter ahead. A stricter test feeds the rule nothing but the shocks and lets it run for a thousand quarters on its own. That is the gold line. It never drifts more than 0.59 percent from the real thing. Approximate aggregation: the mean is nearly enough.

Why does it work? Here is the saving rule of an employed household, next quarter's wealth against this quarter's, with the population drawn beneath it. Except near the bottom, the rule is almost a straight line. And the richer half of households own 74 percent of the capital. Where the rules are straight lines with a common slope, shifting wealth between households does not change their total saving: Gorman's condition from chapter one, holding almost exactly for the households who matter for capital. The poor have curved rules, but they own too little to move the total. That is also when it fails: when the question is about spending rather than capital, the poor and their curved rules are exactly the households who matter.
Continuous: Chapter eight. Continuous time: two equations, one matrix.

In continuous time, the same economy becomes two equations, as Part fifty-one began to show. The first is the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation: the value of holding wealth a with income state j equals the best flow of utility plus how fast that value changes as wealth drifts, plus the chance of switching income. The second is the Kolmogorov forward equation for the density of households: in a steady state, the flow of households out of each small interval of wealth, as their wealth drifts and their income switches, is balanced by the flow in. Both are written with the same drift: income plus interest minus consumption. Yves Achdou, Jiequn Han, Jean-Michel Lasry, Pierre-Louis Lions and Benjamin Moll showed how much that shared piece buys.

Put wealth on a grid. The Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation becomes a matrix equation. Each row of the matrix A says where a household at one grid point goes next: to the neighbouring point up or down, as its wealth drifts, or to the same wealth in the other income state, when its income switches. Nearly every entry is zero. With 1,000 unknowns, at most 3,996 of the 1,000,000 entries are not. And here is the beautiful part: the Kolmogorov forward equation, discretized the same way, uses exactly the same matrix, transposed. The rows that say where each household goes are the columns that say where each household came from. Solve for the value, and the distribution comes almost free.

Here is the solution for Huggett's economy of chapter two. A household with low income runs its bonds down until it reaches the borrowing limit, where its saving stops exactly: in continuous time, the limit binds only at a single point. A household with high income saves, and saves less as it grows richer. One household problem, value and distribution together, takes about 12 milliseconds here. The whole market, found by bisection on the interest rate, 0.20 seconds. That speed is what makes the next step possible: economies hit by shocks, solved again and again.
Hank: Chapter nine. HANK: monetary policy with many households.

HANK stands for Heterogeneous Agent New Keynesian: the households of this part, in an economy where spending sets output, as in Parts twenty-seven and thirty. Here, the households are Aiyagari's, with quarterly periods. Prices are sticky, so firms produce whatever is bought. The central bank sets the real interest rate. The government keeps its debt fixed, so when interest payments fall, taxes fall with them. Any change in spending can be split in two: the direct effect of the interest rate, holding every household's income fixed, and the indirect effect of the change in incomes that comes from everyone else's spending.

Here is the rate cut of the Play it, in the Island's economy, quarter by quarter. Spending jumps by 0.91 percent of output at once and fades with the cut. The direct effect, the response to the rate with incomes held fixed, is the blue line. The indirect effect through incomes is the gold one. In the first quarter the direct effect is 62 percent of the total; over the first year, 45 percent. Within a year, most of the extra spending is people spending incomes that other people's spending created.

Now compare economies. A representative household, with the same rate cut: spending rises by 0.83 percent, and 96 percent of it is direct. That is the textbook. Households with sixteen quarters of income in liquid savings, then four, then just one. Look first at the heights: the totals barely change. Iván Werning showed that, under some conditions, the total response with many households matches the representative household's exactly; here it nearly does. What changes is why. The less liquid wealth households hold, the larger the share that comes through incomes: with one quarter of liquid wealth, only 47 percent is direct. Kaplan, Moll and Violante's economy, with most wealth in illiquid houses and pensions, puts the direct share lower still.

Which economy is right? It turns on how much of a windfall households spend. American households hold several years of income in wealth, but most of it in houses and retirement accounts they cannot easily spend. If all of that wealth were liquid, households here would spend 6 percent of a windfall within the quarter, below the evidence of Part twenty-two, ten to forty percent. If only the liquid part existed, they would spend 49 percent, above it. A one-asset model cannot match both the wealth and the spending. Kaplan and Violante's answer was two assets: many households are wealthy on paper and live hand to mouth, because their wealth is locked in a house or a pension.
Jacobians: Solving a model like this one used to be hard: after a shock the distribution moves, and the old approach linearized the economy in thousands of numbers that describe it. Adrien Auclert, Bence Bardóczy, Matthew Rognlie and Ludwig Straub turned the problem sideways. Treat the households as a single block. Feed it whole paths: the interest rate in each of the next three hundred quarters, and incomes in each quarter. Inside, every household solves its rules backward from the end and the distribution moves forward from today. Out comes the path of total spending. Linearize that map, and it is a matrix: how spending in quarter t responds to income in quarter s. A Jacobian, in the space of sequences.

Here is that matrix for the Island's households, the first forty quarters. Each column is the path of spending after a one-off rise in income in one quarter; each row, a quarter's spending. The bright diagonal says that income is spent mostly when it arrives. Take the first column: income today. Spending jumps at once, then decays over the following quarters, the intertemporal marginal propensities to consume. Take the column for income announced today but paid in quarter ten. Households who can borrow or draw on savings spend some of it before it arrives; those at their limit cannot, so the jump comes when the money does.

Building the matrix one column at a time would mean solving the economy three hundred times. The authors found a shortcut they called the fake-news algorithm. One backward pass records how news about each future quarter changes households' rules today. One forward pass records how a change in next quarter's distribution shows up in spending later. Combined, they give a matrix of the effects of news, and a running sum down its diagonals turns that into the Jacobian. The trick rests on time being the same everywhere: hearing today about quarter s is like hearing next quarter about s minus one, shifted by a quarter.

Does it work? The lines are three columns from the fake-news algorithm. The dots are the same columns computed by brute force, solving the whole economy again with income raised in one quarter. They agree to the fifth decimal place, the error of the small step both use. The difference is the time. All 600 columns, for interest rates and incomes, took 0.47 seconds; by brute force, an estimated 78. Once the Jacobians are in hand, solving the economy's response to any shock is a single linear solve: the equations of chapter nine, each one a matrix.
Policy: Chapter eleven. What changes for policy.

Fiscal policy first. The government buys an extra one percent of output for a while, with the real interest rate held fixed. If it pays with taxes at once, output rises by exactly what the government buys: a multiplier of one, whatever the households are like. Higher taxes and higher incomes cancel for every household. If it borrows and taxes later, the answer depends on who the households are. A representative household sees the future taxes coming and saves for them: the multiplier is still one, as David Ricardo argued. Households with little liquid wealth spend the extra income now and worry about the taxes later. With one quarter of liquid wealth, the multiplier is 1.88. Adrien Auclert, Matthew Rognlie and Ludwig Straub call this the intertemporal Keynesian cross.

Next, promises. The central bank announces a quarter-point cut, for one quarter only, some quarters from now. How much does spending rise today? For a representative household the answer does not depend on how far off the cut is. Its spending today depends on the sum of all future interest rates, and a cut five years away lowers that sum as much as a cut next quarter. Promises about the distant future are as powerful as action now: the forward guidance puzzle. With many households, some of whom may hit their borrowing limits before the cut arrives, distant promises count for less. With one quarter of liquid wealth, a cut five years away does 14 percent less today than one next quarter; with sixteen quarters, 10 percent less. Here the discount is mild. Alisdair McKay, Emi Nakamura and Jón Steinsson showed it can be much stronger when the households most likely to hit their limits face more risk; the puzzle is softened, not solved.

Finally, who gains from inflation? A representative household owes its debts to itself, so a surprise rise in prices moves nothing. Real households hold their debts and their bonds in dollars. Suppose prices rise 5 percent more than anyone expected. A young family with a fixed-rate mortgage of 180,000 dollars gains 8,571 dollars in real terms: the debt is now smaller. A middle-aged couple with a smaller mortgage gains less; a retired teacher with 250,000 dollars in bonds loses 11,905. Matthias Doepke and Martin Schneider measured these positions for the whole United States. The main losers from a moderate inflation are rich, old households, the big bondholders; the winners are young, middle-class households with fixed-rate mortgages, and the government. A representative household cannot even ask the question.
Firms: Chapter twelve. Many firms: entry, exit and lumps.

Households are not the only agents who differ. In 1992 Hugo Hopenhayn built a competitive industry out of a population of firms. A firm pays a cost to enter, and only then learns how productive it is. Each year it hires, produces and pays a fixed cost of operating. Its productivity wanders; when the future is no longer worth the fixed costs, it leaves. Entry continues until entering is worth exactly what it costs, and that pins down the price. In a steady state the industry is constant, but its members are not: each year 6.6 percent of firms are new, and the same share leave. The bars show where the firms are; pink ones stay, red ones are about to go.

Follow one cohort of entrants. Many fail early: after five years 46 percent are still alive, and the failures come mostly in the first few years. The survivors grow: from about 17 workers at entry to 44 by age ten, partly because they get more productive, and partly because the unproductive have left. Up or out: the pattern John Haltiwanger and his coauthors found in American firm data, where young firms are both the most likely to die and the fastest to grow.

Now double the cost of entering, as a licence, a permit or a bank that will not lend might. The price of the good rises, from 4.03 to 4.36. Entry falls from 6.6 to 2.1 percent of firms a year. With fewer challengers, weaker incumbents can afford to stay: the productivity below which firms exit falls from 0.75 to 0.56, and the average firm is 7 percent less productive. A barrier to entry protects the unproductive. A representative firm, which neither enters nor exits, could not show any of this.

One more population. Plants do not invest a little every year; they invest in lumps, because adjusting has fixed costs. Here are three plants: years of nothing, then a burst. In this sketch, 73 percent of plant-years have no investment at all. Add up twenty thousand of them and the lumps vanish: aggregate investment is smooth. But not inert. When a common shock raises every plant's target, many plants cross their thresholds at once, and investment jumps. Whether such lumps matter for the business cycle was the question of Aubhik Khan and Julia Thomas. Their answer, in a general equilibrium where interest rates and wages respond, was that they matter much less than the plants suggest: prices smooth the aggregate further. Heterogeneity is not always decisive; it has to be checked.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: the propensity to spend.

The Dial for this part is the one every model in it turns on: how much of a windfall households spend. It was set in Part twenty-two. The 2001 tax rebates, mailed in an order set by the last digits of Social Security numbers: about thirty percent spent on nondurables within the quarter. The 2008 stimulus payments, about twenty percent, and more counting cars. The 2020 payments, about ten percent, when many households already had cash. Alaska's oil dividend, about a quarter; Italian households asked directly, about half; and Part twenty-two's own households. In Norway, Andreas Fagereng, Martin Holm and Gisle Natvik found that lottery winners with little liquid wealth spent small prizes entirely within the year. The status: it depends on the setting, and most of all on liquidity.

Now ask each model the same question. The representative household spends the interest on a windfall and saves the rest: 0.5 percent in a quarter, far outside the evidence. The households of this part, with liquid wealth from one to sixteen quarters of income: from 49 percent down to 6.5. Only the economies with little liquid wealth land in the range of the evidence. The representative household misses by a factor of twenty or more, and that is why the models of the last three chapters give different answers about monetary and fiscal policy. The amount of wealth matters less than whether it can be spent.
